vocab.definition: A letter (like x or n) that represents a number we don't know yet.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In 3x + 1 = 10, the variable is x.

vocab.definition: A number that does not change. It stays the same in every case.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In T(n) = 3n + 2, the constant is 2.

vocab.definition: The number multiplied by a variable.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In 5x, the coefficient is 5.

vocab.definition: Add up all the values, divide by how many there are. The average.
vocab.subject: math

vocab.definition: The middle value when all numbers are in order.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In 2, 5, 8, 9, 12 — the median is 8.

vocab.definition: The value that appears most often.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In 3, 5, 5, 7, 9 — the mode is 5.

vocab.definition: A comparison between two quantities. How many of one thing for each of another.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 3 red : 5 blue means for every 3 red there are 5 blue.

vocab.definition: Two quantities that increase at the same rate. When one doubles, the other doubles.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Bounce height is proportional to drop height.

vocab.definition: A relationship that makes a straight line on a graph. Constant rate of change.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: y = 2x + 1 is linear. The graph is a straight line.

vocab.definition: How steep a line is. Rise divided by run.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: A line going up 3 for every 1 across has gradient 3.

vocab.definition: The amount added each time in a number sequence.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: In 4, 7, 10, 13... the common difference is 3.

vocab.definition: How much mass is packed into a given volume. Dense things are heavy for their size.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Steel is dense (7.9 g/cm³). Cork is not (0.24 g/cm³).

vocab.definition: The amount of matter in an object. Measured in grams or kilograms.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A 1 kg bag of sugar has the same mass everywhere — even on the Moon.

vocab.definition: The amount of space an object takes up. Measured in cm³ or mL.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A cube 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm has a volume of 1000 cm³.

vocab.definition: A testable prediction about what you think will happen and why.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: If I increase temperature, the reaction rate will increase because particles move faster.

vocab.definition: Something that can change in an experiment. Three types: independent, dependent, controlled.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Independent = what you change. Dependent = what you measure. Controlled = what you keep the same.

vocab.definition: How many times something happens in a given time period. In waves: vibrations per second (Hz).
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A 440 Hz sound wave vibrates 440 times per second.

vocab.definition: The distance between two consecutive peaks (or troughs) of a wave.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.

vocab.definition: The height of a wave from the resting position to the peak. Bigger amplitude = louder/brighter.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A loud sound has a large amplitude. A quiet sound has a small amplitude.

vocab.definition: A community of living things and the non-living environment they interact with.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A pond ecosystem includes fish, plants, water, sunlight, and bacteria.

vocab.definition: A substance that is used up in a chemical reaction. It goes in.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: In burning: fuel + oxygen are reactants.

vocab.definition: A substance that is made in a chemical reaction. It comes out.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: In burning: carbon dioxide + water are products.

vocab.definition: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They make reactions in your body fast enough to keep you alive.

vocab.definition: The process plants use to convert sunlight, water, and CO₂ into glucose and oxygen.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Without photosynthesis, there would be no oxygen in the atmosphere.

vocab.definition: How likely something is to happen. Measured from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 ≈ 0.167.

vocab.definition: Growth that multiplies by the same factor each time. Gets very big very fast.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Bacteria doubling every 20 minutes: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → ...

vocab.definition: Heat transfer through direct contact. Particles vibrate and pass energy to neighbours.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A metal spoon in hot soup gets hot — heat conducts through the metal.

vocab.definition: Heat transfer through fluid movement. Hot fluid rises, cool fluid sinks.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Hot air rises above a radiator, cool air flows in to replace it.

vocab.definition: Heat transfer through electromagnetic waves. No medium needed.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: The Sun heats the Earth through radiation across empty space.

vocab.definition: A pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Only three regular shapes tessellate: triangles, squares, and hexagons.

vocab.definition: A mathematical sentence with an equals sign. Both sides have the same value.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 3x + 1 = 10 is an equation. x = 3 makes both sides equal 10.

vocab.definition: Numbers and letters combined with operations — but NO equals sign.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 3x + 1 is an expression. It is not an equation because there is no = sign.

vocab.definition: A whole number. Can be positive, negative, or zero.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: -3, 0, 7, and 142 are all integers. 0.5 is not.

vocab.definition: Any number that can be written as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 0.75 = 3/4 (rational). π cannot be written as a fraction (irrational).

vocab.definition: A number greater than 1 that has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 are prime. 4 is not (factors: 1, 2, 4).

vocab.definition: A number that divides exactly into another number with no remainder.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: The factors of 12 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

vocab.definition: The result of multiplying a number by any integer.
vocab.subject: math

vocab.definition: The amount of space inside a 2D shape. Measured in square units.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: A rectangle 4cm × 3cm has area = 12 cm².

vocab.definition: The total distance around the outside of a shape.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: A rectangle 4cm × 3cm has perimeter = 14 cm.

vocab.definition: The distance around a circle. Calculated as C = πd or C = 2πr.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: A circle with diameter 10 cm has circumference ≈ 31.4 cm.

vocab.definition: The distance across a circle through the centre. Twice the radius.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: If radius = 5 cm, diameter = 10 cm.

vocab.definition: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge. Half the diameter.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: If diameter = 10 cm, radius = 5 cm.

vocab.definition: Lines that are always the same distance apart. They never meet.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Railway tracks are parallel. They run side by side.

vocab.definition: Lines that meet at exactly 90 degrees (a right angle).
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: The corner of a page is where two perpendicular edges meet.

vocab.definition: When one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other half.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: A butterfly has one line of symmetry — left mirrors right.

vocab.definition: Sliding a shape to a new position without rotating or flipping it.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Move every point 3 right and 2 up: (x,y) → (x+3, y+2).

vocab.definition: Turning a shape around a fixed point by a certain angle.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Rotate 90° clockwise: (x,y) → (y, -x).

vocab.definition: Flipping a shape over a line to create a mirror image.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Reflect in the y-axis: (x,y) → (-x, y).

vocab.definition: The number you multiply by to enlarge or reduce a shape.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Scale factor 2 means every length doubles. Scale factor 0.5 means every length halves.

vocab.definition: An ordered list of numbers that follow a rule.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, ... is a sequence with common difference 3.

vocab.definition: A rule that takes an input and produces exactly one output.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: f(x) = 2x + 1. Input 3 → output 7.

vocab.definition: A statement that one value is greater than, less than, or not equal to another.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: x > 5 means x is any number greater than 5.

vocab.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that describe a position on a grid.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: (3, 5) means 3 across and 5 up from the origin.

vocab.definition: The point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: All coordinates are measured from the origin.

vocab.definition: Where a line crosses an axis. Y-intercept is where x = 0.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: y = 3x + 2 has y-intercept = 2 (the line crosses the y-axis at 2).

vocab.definition: A relationship between two variables. Positive: both increase. Negative: one increases as the other decreases.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Height and shoe size have positive correlation. Temperature and hot chocolate sales have negative correlation.

vocab.definition: A data point that is far away from the others. It does not fit the pattern.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Test scores: 72, 75, 78, 80, 81, 12. The 12 is an outlier.

vocab.definition: The difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset.
vocab.subject: math

vocab.definition: A smaller group selected from a larger population to study.
vocab.subject: math
vocab.example: Asking 50 students about lunch preferences is a sample. The whole school is the population.

vocab.definition: The basic unit of life. All living things are made of cells.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Your body contains about 37 trillion cells. Each one is alive.

vocab.definition: The control centre of a cell. Contains DNA.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: The nucleus tells the cell what proteins to make.

vocab.definition: The powerhouses of the cell. They release energy from glucose through respiration.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Muscle cells have lots of mitochondria because they need lots of energy.

vocab.definition: Found in plant cells only. Where photosynthesis happens.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light and makes plants green.

vocab.definition: The movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Perfume spreading across a room is diffusion — particles move from the bottle to the air.

vocab.definition: The movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Plant roots absorb water by osmosis — water moves from wet soil into the root cells.

vocab.definition: The chemical process that releases energy from glucose in every living cell. Not the same as breathing.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide + Water + Energy. This happens in mitochondria.

vocab.definition: A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded together.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Water (H₂O) is a compound — hydrogen and oxygen bonded together.

vocab.definition: A substance made of only one type of atom. Cannot be broken down further by chemical means.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Gold (Au), oxygen (O), and carbon (C) are elements.

vocab.definition: The smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A gold atom is the smallest piece of gold possible.

vocab.definition: Two or more atoms bonded together.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: O₂ is a molecule (two oxygen atoms). H₂O is also a molecule.

vocab.definition: An atom that has gained or lost electrons, giving it an electrical charge.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Na⁺ is a sodium ion (lost 1 electron). Cl⁻ is a chloride ion (gained 1 electron).

vocab.definition: A scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or alkaline a substance is. 7 is neutral.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Lemon juice ≈ pH 2 (acidic). Water = pH 7 (neutral). Bleach ≈ pH 12 (alkaline).

vocab.definition: A process where reactants are transformed into products. Bonds break and new bonds form.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Burning wood: wood + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + heat.

vocab.definition: A reaction that releases energy (usually heat) to the surroundings.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Burning, neutralisation, and respiration are exothermic — they give out heat.

vocab.definition: A reaction that absorbs energy from the surroundings, making them feel cold.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Photosynthesis and dissolving ammonium nitrate are endothermic.

vocab.definition: The flow of electrical charge through a circuit. Measured in amperes (A).
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: More current = brighter bulb. Current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.

vocab.definition: The push that drives current around a circuit. Measured in volts (V).
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A 12V battery pushes harder than a 1.5V battery. More voltage = more current (if resistance stays the same).

vocab.definition: How much a component opposes the flow of current. Measured in ohms (Ω).
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A thin wire has more resistance than a thick wire. More resistance = less current.

vocab.definition: A push or a pull. Measured in newtons (N). Can change speed, direction, or shape.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Gravity pulls you down (your weight in N). The floor pushes you up (normal force).

vocab.definition: The force of attraction between any two masses. On Earth: 9.8 N/kg.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A 1 kg object weighs about 9.8 N on Earth but only 1.6 N on the Moon.

vocab.definition: A force that opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Rough surfaces have more friction. Ice has very little friction.

vocab.definition: How fast something is moving. Distance divided by time.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: If you run 100m in 12.5 seconds, your speed = 100 ÷ 12.5 = 8 m/s.

vocab.definition: How quickly speed is changing. Measured in m/s².
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Going from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 seconds = acceleration of 4 m/s².

vocab.definition: The energy an object has because it is moving. KE = ½mv².
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A fast car has more kinetic energy than a slow one. Doubling speed quadruples KE.

vocab.definition: Stored energy due to position or condition. Gravitational PE = mgh.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A ball held high has gravitational PE. When dropped, PE converts to KE.

vocab.definition: Giant slabs of rock that make up Earth's surface. They move slowly over the mantle.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: The Pacific Plate moves about 7-10 cm per year — roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

vocab.definition: A sudden shaking of the ground caused by tectonic plate movement.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Earthquakes happen at plate boundaries where plates push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.

vocab.definition: An opening in Earth's crust where molten rock (magma) reaches the surface.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Volcanoes often form at subduction zones where one plate slides under another.

vocab.definition: The wearing away and transport of rock and soil by wind, water, or ice.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Rivers erode their banks. Glaciers carve valleys. Wind shapes desert rocks.

vocab.definition: The breaking down of rock in place — without movement. Physical, chemical, or biological.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Freeze-thaw: water gets into cracks, freezes, expands, and breaks the rock apart.

vocab.definition: The preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms found in rock.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Fossils of the same species on different continents are evidence that the continents were once joined.

vocab.definition: The process where organisms better adapted to their environment survive and reproduce more.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Darker moths survived better on soot-covered trees during the Industrial Revolution.

vocab.definition: A feature of an organism that helps it survive in its environment.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A camel's hump stores fat (not water). Long eyelashes keep out sand. Both are adaptations to desert life.

vocab.definition: A sequence showing what eats what. Energy flows from producer to consumers.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Grass → Rabbit → Fox → Eagle. Each arrow means 'is eaten by'.

vocab.definition: An organism that makes its own food from sunlight (photosynthesis). Always at the start of a food chain.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Grass, trees, algae, and phytoplankton are all producers.

vocab.definition: An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Primary consumers eat producers. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers.

vocab.definition: An organism that breaks down dead matter, returning nutrients to the soil.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers. Without them, dead material would pile up forever.

vocab.definition: The variety of different species in an area. Higher biodiversity = healthier ecosystem.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A tropical rainforest has high biodiversity. A monoculture farm has very low biodiversity.

vocab.definition: The natural environment where an organism lives.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: A pond is a habitat for frogs. A desert is a habitat for cacti.

vocab.definition: The specific role an organism plays in its ecosystem — what it eats, where it lives, when it is active.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Two species cannot occupy the same niche in the same habitat for long — one will outcompete the other.

vocab.definition: Energy from sources that are naturally replenished. Will not run out.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: Solar, wind, hydroelectric, and geothermal are renewable. Coal and gas are not.

vocab.definition: When certain gases trap heat in the atmosphere, warming the planet.
vocab.subject: science
vocab.example: CO₂ and methane are greenhouse gases. Some greenhouse effect is natural and necessary. Too much causes warming.
